title: Still-Life with Nine Objects
altText: A black-and-white etching of a still life, a group of nine objects set close together on a surface. It is made of fine lines and shading rather than color.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist (Giorgio Morandi, Italian, 1890-1964), date, medium, place of origin, credit line and public-domain flag (false) read from the record. The record has no description or subject terms, and its image text only repeats the medium. No image linked because the work is in copyright.

context: Made in 1954 by the Italian artist Giorgio Morandi, who is widely known for quiet still lifes of simple household objects. The museum record lists the medium as etching on cream wove paper and the title as Still-Life with Nine Objects; it offers no further description of the print.

descriptions.k: This is a picture of nine objects sitting together. It is a print made with lines, in black and white. Can you count the objects? Which two stand closest to each other?
descriptions.g12: Giorgio Morandi made this print of nine objects sitting together on a table. It uses only lines and shading, with no color. The objects are grouped close like friends. Can you count them? What do you think each one might be?
descriptions.g35: Giorgio Morandi, from Italy, was famous for quiet pictures of simple objects. This one is an etching, a print made by scratching lines into metal, then inking it. It shows nine objects grouped closely, using only black lines on cream paper. How can lines alone show shape and shadow? Why might an artist keep a picture so simple?
descriptions.g68: Morandi made Still-Life with Nine Objects in 1954 as an etching, a print made by cutting lines into a metal plate. The museum gives only the title and medium, so the picture must be read from what you see: a close group of objects drawn with lines and shading on cream paper. How can lines create volume and shadow? Why might such an ordinary subject be worth so much attention?
descriptions.g910: Morandi's 1954 etching Still-Life with Nine Objects reduces a familiar subject, a group of everyday things, to line, tone, and arrangement. The museum offers no commentary beyond the title and medium, so meaning rests on what the print visibly does with its objects. Consider how closeness, overlap, and shading build a small world, and how limiting the work to black line on cream paper focuses attention on relationships rather than things.
descriptions.g1112: Still-Life with Nine Objects (1954) shows Morandi's persistent, narrow focus: a small group of objects, rendered in etched line on cream paper. The museum's record is minimal, so interpretation depends on the print's formal evidence. Critics often describe Morandi's work as meditative, yet such labels can overreach. How do line density, spacing, and overlap of the nine objects create meaning, and what does repetition of a limited subject over a career suggest about artistic purpose?

k.daily: How many objects can you count? Which one do you like best?
k.emotion: Does this picture feel quiet or noisy? What makes you say so?
k.observation: Which objects look tall and which look short?
k.analysis: What do you see first? Why do you think your eyes go there?
k.line: Find a line that goes straight and a line that curves. Where are they?
k.shape: Look for round shapes and tall shapes. Where do you find each one?
k.color: The picture has no color. What colors would you add, and where?
k.texture: This print is made with lots of tiny lines. Where do the lines look thick and dark?
k.space: Which objects are close together and which are apart?
k.light: Which objects look lit up, and which sit in shadow?
k.meaning: The title says nine objects. What could they be?
k.culture: Which everyday things do you see at home that are like these objects?
k.technique: An etching is made by scratching lines. How would you make dark and light with just lines?
k.personal: If you grouped nine objects from your desk, which would you choose?
k.critical: Why might an artist like to draw simple, everyday things?

g12.daily: What might the nine objects be? Use their shapes as clues.
g12.emotion: What feeling does a picture of calm, quiet objects give you?
g12.observation: List what you see: shapes, lines, light, dark. What did you notice last?
g12.analysis: How are the objects grouped together? Which ones overlap?
g12.line: How do the many tiny lines make some places look dark?
g12.shape: Which shapes are tall, short, round, or square? How do they fit together?
g12.color: This picture has only black lines on cream paper. How does that change what you notice?
g12.texture: How do lines close together look different from lines far apart?
g12.space: Which objects look closer to you and which look farther away?
g12.light: Where does the light seem to come from? How do you know?
g12.meaning: Why might an artist use the same kinds of objects again and again?
g12.culture: Morandi lived in Italy. What everyday objects might people have in their homes there?
g12.technique: An etching is made by cutting lines into metal. How is that different from drawing with pencil?
g12.personal: Choose three objects at home to draw. How would you arrange them?
g12.critical: Does a picture of simple things have to be boring? Explain using this one.

g35.daily: What can you tell about these objects from their outlines and shadows alone?
g35.emotion: How would you describe the mood of this still life?
g35.observation: Look slowly. Which small area of lines or shading did you notice late?
g35.analysis: How does Morandi place nine objects so the group looks like one shape?
g35.line: How do the direction and thickness of lines build each object's form?
g35.shape: How do overlapping shapes help create a sense of a group?
g35.color: The print has no color. How do light and dark take color's place?
g35.texture: How do dense lines produce dark areas and open paper produce light areas?
g35.space: How does he show depth when everything sits so closely together?
g35.light: How does shading hint at where the light is coming from?
g35.meaning: Morandi painted and printed similar objects many times. What might he have wanted to learn by looking so closely?
g35.culture: Etching was used by artists for centuries. How does Morandi use an old method for a quiet modern subject?
g35.technique: Why might he have chosen the exact objects and spacing he did?
g35.personal: How would the mood change if the objects were scattered across the page?
g35.critical: Why might some people find a quiet picture like this more interesting than a busy one?

g68.daily: What might the arrangement of nine objects suggest about how Morandi saw ordinary things?
g68.emotion: How does the lack of color affect the mood of the print?
g68.observation: What does the museum tell you, and what must you work out for yourself from the image?
g68.analysis: How does the grouping, overlap, and spacing of the objects create a composition?
g68.line: How do hatching and cross-hatching, if you see them, build form?
g68.shape: How do simple shapes repeat and vary across the group?
g68.color: How does the limited tonal range, black on cream, affect the way you see the objects?
g68.texture: How does the etched line differ in character from a painted brushstroke?
g68.space: How does he create a shallow stage with limited depth?
g68.light: How does shading imply a single gentle light?
g68.meaning: Why might an artist repeat the same sort of subject, and what could that teach?
g68.culture: How might Morandi's quiet approach have contrasted with the noisy politics and change of mid-twentieth-century Europe?
g68.technique: How does an etching require planning because lines cannot be easily erased?
g68.personal: How would you compose a still life from objects in your own home?
g68.critical: Can a small, quiet artwork be as important as a large dramatic one? Explain.

g910.daily: How does Morandi convey a feeling of quiet or contemplation without any narrative?
g910.emotion: How does the lack of color shift attention toward tone and structure?
g910.observation: Analyze how overlaps and intervals among the nine objects form a unified composition.
g910.analysis: How does line density create volume, shadow, and surface?
g910.line: How do the geometric simplifications of the objects relate to modernist abstraction?
g910.shape: How do limited tonal contrasts create subtle emphasis?
g910.color: How does the etching technique shape the character of the lines?
g910.texture: How does the shallow space focus attention on relationships rather than setting?
g910.space: How does the print suggest light, and why might it be diffuse rather than dramatic?
g910.light: The museum gives only a title and medium. What responsibilities do viewers have when interpreting such a work?
g910.meaning: How does Morandi's persistent attention to everyday objects challenge ideas of what is worthy of art?
g910.culture: How does working in printmaking differ from painting for this subject?
g910.technique: What might it mean for an artist to explore a small subject deeply rather than many subjects broadly?
g910.personal: How does the print's intimacy affect how you stand and look?
g910.critical: How should we assess an artwork that deliberately avoids spectacle?

g1112.daily: How does the print reduce the world to relationships of form, and what does that imply about perception?
g1112.emotion: How does the stripped-down vocabulary of line and tone support or complicate descriptions of Morandi as meditative?
g1112.observation: Separate the formal evidence in the print from the biographical narrative commonly told about Morandi.
g1112.analysis: How does the clustering of the objects create a compositional unity that resembles architecture?
g1112.line: How does the line's density, direction, and edge produce volume without color?
g1112.shape: How does the print position itself between representation and abstraction?
g1112.color: How does tonal restraint heighten sensitivity to small variations?
g1112.texture: How does etching's mediated, incised line shape the relationship between hand and image?
g1112.space: How does the compressed space refuse conventional perspectival depth?
g1112.light: How does the handling of light produce stillness rather than drama?
g1112.meaning: With minimal museum commentary, how can interpretation remain responsible, and where does it become projection?
g1112.culture: How does Morandi's repeated engagement with a narrow motif complicate narratives of artistic progress and novelty?
g1112.technique: How might his quiet practice be read in relation to the upheavals of his era without being illustrative of them?
g1112.personal: How do your own habits of attention change when facing an artwork with so little overt content?
g1112.critical: What does this print suggest about the value of looking closely at the familiar?

safety.method: Title, artist and medium (etching) checked against the Art Institute of Chicago record; a still life of objects with no concerning terms. The record has no description of the imagery, so student text relies on the title and medium. The image itself was not visually inspected.

teacherNote.context: A 1954 etching by the Italian artist Giorgio Morandi in the Art Institute of Chicago. The museum record gives only the title and medium, so this entry is cautious and a person must review the image. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students set up a still life of five or more objects and draw it using only lines for shading.
Discuss why an artist might use the same simple subject many times.
Compare how a print and a pencil drawing show light and dark differently.
